package_info.why_malicious: The plugin generates and displays a fraudulent ransomware notice on WordPress sites, attempting to extort website owners by demanding cryptocurrency payment for file recovery, despite no actual encryption or data loss occurring. This constitutes a social engineering attack and extortion attempt via malicious code.

execution_context.trigger: on page load (when site is accessed by owner or visitor)
execution_context.file_location: WordPress plugin-generated HTML file served in the site's root directory or as a replacement for the homepage
required_permissions: filesystem (write or overwrite HTML files in web root)
webserver (serve modified or new HTML content to users)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
Your website has been encrypted!

To recover your files, send 0.1 bitcoin to the following address...
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: On page load, the code serves a static HTML ransom note by overwriting or replacing the site's homepage, presenting a fake message about file encryption and demanding cryptocurrency payment, with no actual file encryption or data modification performed.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code displays a ransom note claiming the website has been encrypted and demands payment, but there is no evidence of any file encryption or legitimate administrative action. The presence of extortion language and cryptocurrency payment instructions is a clear indicator of malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate WordPress plugin should never generate or display ransom/extortion messages, nor should it overwrite or replace site content with fraudulent notices. Plugins are expected to enhance functionality, not engage in social engineering or extortion.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate plugins may display maintenance or informational banners, but these never include false claims of encryption or demands for payment. Any plugin presenting such messages is acting outside the bounds of normal plugin behavior.
key_indicators: HTML content containing phrases such as 'Your website has been encrypted!' and cryptocurrency payment instructions
No corresponding file encryption or modification activity detected
Overwriting or replacing the site's homepage or key HTML files with ransom note content
Presence of static or hardcoded cryptocurrency addresses in plugin-generated files

attack_chain.action: Attacker uploads and installs a bogus WordPress plugin on target websites, either via compromised admin credentials or exploiting plugin upload functionality.
attack_chain.leads_to: Plugin is present and activated on the WordPress site.

attack_chain.action: Upon activation, the plugin generates and writes a static HTML ransom note file, overwriting or replacing the site's homepage or key entry point.
attack_chain.leads_to: The ransom note is now served to site owners and visitors.

attack_chain.action: When the site is accessed, the ransom note HTML is displayed, falsely claiming the website has been encrypted and demanding cryptocurrency payment.
attack_chain.leads_to: Site owners may be deceived into paying the ransom, despite no actual encryption or data loss.

behavioral_signatures: WordPress plugin generating or overwriting HTML files with ransom/extortion content
Display of ransom or extortion messages on the homepage or key site entry points without any file encryption activity
Sudden replacement of legitimate site content with static ransom note HTML
file_indicators: HTML files in the web root or plugin directories containing phrases like 'Your website has been encrypted!' or cryptocurrency payment instructions
Unexpected new or modified index.html, index.php, or similar files with ransom note content
Presence of static cryptocurrency addresses in plugin-generated files
network_indicators: No direct network indicators unless the plugin attempts to contact an external server or verify payment; otherwise, only the presence of cryptocurrency addresses in served content
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for new or modified HTML files in the WordPress root or plugin directories containing ransom/extortion language or cryptocurrency payment instructions. Flag plugins that generate, overwrite, or serve such content. Correlate with the absence of file encryption or modification activity to identify fake ransomware attempts. Review plugin code for hardcoded ransom note templates or cryptocurrency addresses.
